hook: A cyclist on a hilly road knows she has reached the top of a climb when the road stops going up and starts going down. A flat stretch alone does not prove it: the road may level off and keep climbing. The First Derivative Test turns that common sense into a rule you can state and justify.

prereq.q: If $f'(x) > 0$ on an interval, then on that interval $f$ is
prereq.why: A positive derivative means rising tangent lines.

prereq.q: Which points are critical points of $f$?
options: Interior points where $f' = 0$ or $f'$ does not exist
prereq.why: Relative extrema can occur only at critical points.

figure.caption: At a critical point $c$, the change in the sign of $f'$ decides: $+$ to $-$ is a peak, $-$ to $+$ a valley, and no change means no extremum.

chain.cause: $f'$ changes from positive to negative at a critical point $c$ (and $f$ is continuous at $c$)
chain.effect: $f$ rises up to $c$ and falls after it, so $f(c)$ is a relative maximum

chain.cause: $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $c$
chain.effect: $f$ falls then rises, so $f(c)$ is a relative minimum

chain.cause: $f'$ has the same sign on both sides of $c$
chain.effect: $f$ keeps rising (or falling) through $c$: no relative extremum, even if $f'(c) = 0$
write the sentence: "$f'$ changes from negative to positive at $x = c$, so $f$ has a relative minimum there"

ideas: First Derivative Test: at a critical point $c$ where $f$ is continuous, if $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$, $f(c)$ is a relative maximum; from $-$ to $+$, a relative minimum; no change, neither.
It works where $f'$ does not exist (corners, cusps) as well as where $f' = 0$.
A sign chart of $f'$ organizes the work, but it is not a justification by itself: write the sentence.
On a graph of $f'$: a relative maximum of $f$ is where the graph of $f'$ crosses the axis going down; a minimum, crossing going up. Touching without crossing gives nothing.

misconception.wrong: $f'(c) = 0$, so $f$ has a relative maximum or minimum at $c$.
misconception.right: The scoring guidelines give no credit for "$f'(c) = 0$" alone. The point needs a sign change, stated with its direction: "$f'$ changes from positive to negative at $x = c$." For $x^3$ at 0, $f' = 0$ but there is no extremum.

summary: At a critical point, look at the sign of $f'$ on each side. $+$ to $-$: relative maximum. $-$ to $+$: relative minimum. No change: no extremum. The test works where $f'$ is undefined too. Justify in words that name $f'$ and the direction of its sign change; a sign chart alone does not earn the point.
